extracted.intended_audience: educated readers, critics, and aspiring philosophers/authors reading or writing philosophical works
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for how to read, judge, and approach the writing (and moral decisions about) philosophical and literary works—when to read, when to skip, what capacities are required, and methodological postulates for philosophical inquiry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thorough self-examination before decisive action
rubrics_metrics.description: Before taking an irreversible step (e.g., leaving an established profession for authorship), ascertain with strict self-examination whether other influences are at work; catalogue scruples; ensure you have read the best and most fundamental works; have both mind and heart opened to illustrious examples; consult elder contemporaries who have acted on similar scruples.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Delay important decisions: 'Time spent in such delay is time won'—allow manhood, knowledge, judgment, and temperance to grow; this prevents decisions being alloyed by rashness or vanity. Seek precedents of those who changed course and later found the error of their deviation. Avoid acting from impatience or the illusion that authorship carries fewer temptations than other professions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid excessive or premature authorship
rubrics_metrics.description: Herder's warning: 'Am sorgfaeltigsten, meiden sie die Autorschaft. Zu frueh oder unmaessig gebraucht, macht sie den Kopf wueste and das Herz leer,' i.e., authorship, used too early or immoderately, makes the head wild and the heart empty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not read only to publish; indiscriminate or constant publication reduces quality and turns one into 'a mere servant of the printing press'—maintain selectivity and inward cultivation rather than ceaseless output.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reading maxim: presume your ignorance of a writer's understanding until you understand his ignorance
rubrics_metrics.description: In the perusal of philosophical works: 'until you understand a writer’s ignorance, presume yourself ignorant of his understanding.' If you can trace the grounds of a visionary's errors to bodily causes you may explain them without accusing intentional falsehood; if you cannot reconcile apparent genius with unintelligible passages, assume your own ignorance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply charitable analysis: attempt to explain an author's errors by intelligible causes before dismissing him; where explanation fails (e.g., obscure Platonic passages), humility requires assuming your own lack of comprehension rather than contempt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read whole and connectedly rather than by detached excerpts
rubrics_metrics.description: Either pass over the following chapter altogether, or read the whole connectedly: 'The fairest part of the most beautiful body will appear deformed and monstrous, if dissevered from its place in the organic whole.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not judge delicate philosophical material from piecemeal quotations—separating ideas from their forms risks producing a 'skeleton' that misrepresents and alarms; context is essential for faithful understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion to judge whether a treatise is suitable for a reader
rubrics_metrics.description: If a reader receives as fundamental, indemonstrable facts the general notions (matter, spirit, soul, body, action, passiveness, time, space, cause and effect, consciousness, perception, memory and habit) and is satisfied by reducing other notions into these elements, then the chapter was not written for him.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this as a practical pre-screen: those who unthinkingly accept basic metaphysical categories as final will find transcendental/philosophical works unproductive and should refrain from detailed study of such treatises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid reducing philosophy to terminological analysis only
rubrics_metrics.description: Merely taking the 'general notions' in mass and reducing other notions into them (an analysis of terms) does not add to knowledge; it prepares but does not constitute philosophy in its highest sense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Philosophy must aim at 'intuitive' or 'immediate' knowledge beyond mere logical manipulation of terms; analysis is useful as discipline but insufficient for ultimate truths.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject compendious empiricism that equates mind with impressions
rubrics_metrics.description: Criticism of 'compendious philosophy' that talks of mind but thinks of 'brick and mortar'—theory of spirit by nicknaming matter and reducing everything to impressions, ideas, and sensations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be wary of philosophies that collapse spiritual realities into mere sensations; they cannot reach the transcendental domain and will leave the reader with an impoverished account of inner sense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of postulates/primary intuitions in philosophy analogous to geometry
rubrics_metrics.description: Philosophy must introduce postulates (primary constructions) as mathematics does; the most original construction or first productive act for the inner sense must be postulated rather than demonstrated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accept that some starting points must be taken as primary (intuitions or postulates) for philosophical systems to proceed; these are analogous to geometric primitives and are necessary for evidence in philosophical argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: The direction of the inner sense is an act of freedom
rubrics_metrics.description: The inner sense's direction is determined chiefly by an act of freedom: different persons develop different inner orientations (sensations, forms, notions, reflection).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize the practical/moral component of philosophical cultivation: developing the 'philosophic organ' requires voluntary discipline and moral effort, not merely intellectual training.

rubrics_metrics.name: Philosophic capacity test: Know thyself
rubrics_metrics.description: The postulate of philosophy and test of philosophic capacity is 'KNOW THYSELF'—both practically and speculatively; philosophy is science of being and its first ground must be both practical and speculative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Self-intuition and self-reflection (immediate consciousness) are prerequisites for engagement in transcendental philosophy; without them, philosophical discourse remains lifeless.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain methodological purity between natural and transcendental approaches
rubrics_metrics.description: When pursuing sciences that start from object (natural philosophy) or subject (transcendental philosophy), adhere strictly to that science's principles and exclude principles of the opposite science (avoid importing subjective suppositions into natural philosophy and objective reduction into transcendental philosophy).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enforce a disciplined scepticism that purifies the method: natural philosophers must avoid occult qualities/final causes; transcendental philosophers must avoid importing sensory-impression models (e.g., retinal pictures) as explanatory primitives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thesis I — Truth is correlative to being
rubrics_metrics.description: Truth is correlative to being: knowledge without a correspondent reality is no knowledge; 'To know is in its very essence a verb active.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate claims by whether there is a correspondent reality; avoid accepting mere abstractions or representations as knowledge when they lack grounding in being.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thesis II — Distinguish immediate and mediate truth
rubrics_metrics.description: All truth is either mediate (derived from other truths) or immediate and original (absolute: formula A. A.); mediate truth is conditional (formula B. A.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When constructing or critiquing arguments, be explicit about whether a claim is asserted as immediate (self-evident/axiomatic) or mediate (dependent); trace the dependence (B → A) to understand the certainty attached to conclusions.
